newsitem.title: DENMARK: Analysts welcome Danish first quarter GDP data.
newsitem.headline: Analysts welcome Danish first quarter GDP data.

text.p: Danish analysts on Monday welcomed first quarter 1997 Gross Domestic Product data as showing a balanced economy and good export prospects.
The National Statistics Office earlier announced year on year first quarter growth of 2.4 percent, compared to average analysts' forecasts of 3.4 percent.

"It's a good number that gives a harmonious picture of the Danish economy. There is more restrained domestic demand than we expected and exports are stronger," Den Danske Bank's Per Hviid told Reuters.
"That means that in all the places where one might before have been worried there are now grounds to be less concerned," he added.

Monday's figures showed GDP shrinking by 0.1 percent between the first quarter of 1997 and the last three months of 1996 and also revised the full-year 1996 figure to 2.7 percent, from an earlier 2.4 percent.
It logged quarterly growth of 0.8 percent in imports of goods and services during the first three months of 1997, compared with 3.7 percent export growth.
In the fourth quarter the respective figures were 1.7 percent and 2.2 percent up from the preceeding three months.
"Everything shows strong exports, so we can look foward to continued high exports in the second quarter, with a greater contribution to GDP," Nykredit Bank's Henrik Asmussen said.
"It all looks very reasonable...it indicates continuing moderate progress in the Danish economy," he added.
Svenska Handelsbanken agreed that the figures showed well-balanced growth and added that it was sticking to its existing predictions for 1997 and 1998 GDP.

"We are maintaining our growth forecasts for 3.5 percent this year and 3.0 percent next year but we are much more positive about inflation and the balance of payments," the bank's chief economist, Bo Overvad said.
But Unibank took a more cautious line saying that the economy was still in danger of overheating.
Senior analyst Jesper Nielsen said that a first quarter fall in gross investments of three percent from the preceeding three months might be reversed in the second quarter.
"And unemployment figures don't indicate a slowdown in economic activity," he added.
May unemployment was 8.1 percent, compared to 8.9 percent in May 1996.
